title: מַסֶּכֶת אָבוֹת — פֶּרֶק שְׁלִישִׁי
part: Chapter 3 · Akavya ben Mahalalel to Rabbi Elazar Ḥisma
draftNote: The text follows the Wikisource transcription of the Kaufmann manuscript, apart from the editorial steps named in the source note; the prepared audio is being recorded; a check against the manuscript photographs is still to come. Use ⚑ correction on any mishnah to report a problem.
source: Text: the Kaufmann manuscript of the Mishnah (Budapest, Library of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, Kaufmann A 50), fols. 169r–173v, from the diplomatic transcription on Hebrew Wikisource (כתב יד קאופמן למשנה/מסכת אבות, CC BY-SA 4.0), which records the work of the later hands. The vowel points are the manuscript's own. Where it leaves a letter of a pointed word bare, the editor has supplied the point, and the mishnah's note lists every such word; words the manuscript leaves wholly unpointed stay unpointed. Reading text: the manuscript as corrected. Letters the manuscript erases are omitted; corrections and additions by later hands, including marginal ones, are printed; marginal variant readings (נ״א) are left out. Words the scribe broke across a line end are rejoined. The scribe's abbreviations are kept, marked with a geresh (׳), and expanded in the glossary. The transcription writes Kaufmann's ḥolam, which sits over the preceding letter, as a dot on that letter; it is given here as an ordinary ḥolam. Mishnayot are numbered as in the standard printed editions; where Kaufmann divides differently, or lacks a mishnah, the note says so. Romanization: simplified, following Modern Israeli pronunciation. Pronunciation convention: Modern Israeli Hebrew applied to Kaufmann's vowels — an admitted choice, since the manuscript's pointing reflects an older Palestinian tradition. Translations made fresh from the Hebrew and Aramaic; no modern translation consulted. Audio: Google Cloud TTS, Modern Israeli Hebrew voice, reading the pointed text; abbreviations are read in full (או׳ as אוֹמֵר, שנ׳ as שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר, the divine name as Adonay).
about: Avot, "Fathers", is the tractate of the Mishnah made up of maxims; the rest of the Mishnah is law. It opens with the chain of tradition from Moses at Sinai to the Men of the Great Assembly, then gives the sayings of the sages from the early pairs down to the generation of the Mishnah's editor, Rabbi Judah the Prince. The Mishnah was compiled around 200 CE. Many communities read Avot a chapter at a time on Sabbath afternoons between Passover and Shavuot, and often through the summer, adding a sixth chapter, Kinyan Torah, to make six weeks. Chapters 1–5 here follow a single manuscript, the Kaufmann codex, probably copied in Italy in the eleventh or twelfth century and the best witness to the Mishnah's own Hebrew. It reads differently from the familiar printed text in many small places, and the notes point them out.

sentences.t: עֲקַבְיָה בֶן מַהֲלַלְאֵל אוֹמ׳ הִיסְתְּכֵּל בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה דְבָרִים וְאֵין אַתָּה בָא לִידֵי עֲבֵירָה דַּע מֵאַיִין בָּאתָה וּלְאַיין אַתָּה הוֹלֵךְ וְלִפְנֵי מִי אַתָּה עָתִיד לִיתֵּן דִּין וְחֶשְׁבּוֹן דַּע מֵנַיִן בָּאתָה מִלֵּחָה סְרוּחָה וּלְאַיִן אַתָּה הוֹלֵךְ לְרִימָּה וּלְתוֹלֵיעָה וְלִפְנֵי מִי אַתָּה עָתִיד לִיתֵן דִּין וְחֶשְׁבּוֹן לִפְנֵי מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים הַקָבָּ״הֻ
sentences.tr: Akavya ben Mahalalel omer: histakel bi-shlosha dvarim ve-ein ata va lidei avera. Da me-ayin bata, u-le-ayin ata holekh, ve-lifnei mi ata atid liten din ve-ḥeshbon. Da menayin bata: mi-leḥa sruḥa; u-le-ayin ata holekh: le-rima u-le-tole'a; ve-lifnei mi ata atid liten din ve-ḥeshbon: lifnei melekh malkhei ha-mlakhim, ha-Kadosh barukh hu.
sentences.l: Akavya son of Mahalalel says: look into three things, and you do not come into the hands of transgression. Know from-where you came, and to-where you are going, and before whom you are destined to give judgment and account. Know from-where you came: from a putrid fluid; and to-where you are going: to the worm and to the maggot; and before whom you are destined to give judgment and account: before the King of the kings of the kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.
sentences.i: Akavya ben Mahalalel says: Keep three things in view and you will not fall into sin. Know where you came from, where you are going, and before whom you will one day give a full reckoning. Where you came from: a putrid fluid. Where you are going: to worm and maggot. Before whom you will give a full reckoning: before the King of the king of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.
sentences.n: דִּין וְחֶשְׁבּוֹן, 'judgment and account', is a pair meaning a full reckoning. Persian rulers called themselves 'king of kings'; God is the King above them. The putrid fluid is semen. Kaufmann's answers differ from the printed text: it has מִלֵּחָה סְרוּחָה, 'from a putrid fluid', where the printed text has מִטִּפָּה סְרוּחָה, 'from a putrid drop', and לְרִימָּה וּלְתוֹלֵיעָה, 'to worm and maggot', where the printed text has לִמְקוֹם עָפָר רִמָּה וְתוֹלֵעָה, 'to a place of dust, worm and maggot'. Spellings to notice: מֵאַיִין with a doubled yod, בָּאתָה for בָּאתָ, and מֵנַיִן beside מֵאַיִן for 'from where'. The scribe wrote לפני once too often before the second דַּע and erased it. Vowel points supplied by the editor where the manuscript leaves a letter bare: הִיסְתְּכֵּל, בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה.
sentences.say: עֲקַבְיָה בֶן מַהֲלַלְאֵל אוֹמֵר הִיסְתְּכֵּל בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה דְבָרִים וְאֵין אַתָּה בָא לִידֵי עֲבֵירָה דַּע מֵאַיִין בָּאתָה וּלְאַיין אַתָּה הוֹלֵךְ וְלִפְנֵי מִי אַתָּה עָתִיד לִיתֵּן דִּין וְחֶשְׁבּוֹן דַּע מֵנַיִן בָּאתָה מִלֵּחָה סְרוּחָה וּלְאַיִן אַתָּה הוֹלֵךְ לְרִימָּה וּלְתוֹלֵיעָה וְלִפְנֵי מִי אַתָּה עָתִיד לִיתֵן דִּין וְחֶשְׁבּוֹן לִפְנֵי מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים הַקָּדוֹשׁ-בָּרוּךְ-הוּא

sentences.t: ר׳ חֲנַנְיָה סְגַן הַכֹּהֲנִים אוֹ׳ הֱוֵוי מִתְפַּלֵּל בִּשְׁלֹמָהּ שֶׁלַּמַּלְכוּת שֶׁאִילּוּלֵי מוֹרָאָה אִישׁ אֶת רְעֵהוּ חַיִּים בָּלַעְנוּ: ר׳ חֲנַנְיָה בֶן תַּרְדְּיוֹן או׳ שְׁנַיִם שֶׁהָיוּ יוֹשְׁבִים וְאֵין בֵּינֵיהֶן דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה הֲרֵי זֶה מוֹשַׁב לֵיצִים שנ׳ וּבְמוֹשַׁב לֵיצִים לֹא יָשָׁב אֲבָל שְׁנַיִם שֶׁיּוֹשְׁבִים וַעֲסוּקִים בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה שְׁכִינָה בֵינֵיהֶם שנ׳ אָז נִדְבְּרוּ יִרְאֵי יָ׳י אִישׁ אֶל רְעֵהוּ וַיַּקְשֵׁב יָ׳י וַיּשְׁמַע וַיִּכָּתֵב סֵפֶר זִכָּרוֹן לְפָנָיו לְיִרְאֵי יָ״י וּלְחֹשְׁבֵי שְׁמוֹ
sentences.tr: Rabi Ḥananya sgan ha-kohanim omer: hevei mitpalel bi-shlomah shel ha-malkhut, she-ilulei mora'ah ish et re'ehu ḥayim bala'nu. Rabi Ḥananya ben Teradyon omer: shnayim she-hayu yoshvim ve-ein beineihen divrei tora, harei ze moshav letsim, she-ne'emar: u-ve-moshav letsim lo yashav. Aval shnayim she-yoshvim va-asukim be-divrei tora, shkhina beineihem, she-ne'emar: az nidberu yir'ei Adonay ish el re'ehu, va-yakshev Adonay va-yishma, va-yikatev sefer zikaron lefanav le-yir'ei Adonay u-le-ḥoshvei shmo.
sentences.l: Rabbi Ḥananya, deputy of the priests, says: be praying for the welfare of the kingdom, for were-it-not-for fear-of-it, a man his fellow alive we would-have-swallowed. Rabbi Ḥananya son of Teradyon says: two who were sitting and there are no words of Torah between them, behold this is a seat of scoffers, as it is said: 'and in the seat of scoffers he did not sit.' But two who sit and are occupied with words of Torah, the Presence is between them, as it is said: 'Then those who fear the LORD spoke a man to his fellow, and the LORD listened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before Him for those who fear the LORD and for those who think on His name.'
sentences.i: Rabbi Ḥananya, the deputy high priest, says: Pray for the welfare of the government, for without the fear of it we would swallow one another alive. Rabbi Ḥananya ben Teradyon says: When two sit together and no words of Torah pass between them, that is a session of scoffers, as it is said, 'nor sat in the seat of scoffers' (Psalm 1:1). But when two sit and occupy themselves with words of Torah, the Divine Presence rests between them, as it is said, 'Then those who feared the LORD talked with one another; the LORD took note and listened, and a book of remembrance was written before Him for those who fear the LORD and give thought to His name' (Malachi 3:16).
sentences.n: The סְגַן הַכֹּהֲנִים, 'deputy of the priests', was the officer next in rank to the high priest in the Temple's last decades. Ḥananya ben Teradyon was executed by the Romans in the Hadrianic persecution (c. 135 CE) for teaching Torah in public. שְׁכִינָה, literally 'dwelling', is the rabbinic name for God's presence among people. Kaufmann reads בָּלַעְנוּ, 'we would have swallowed', where the printed text has בְּלָעוֹ, 'would swallow him'; the manuscript's wording echoes Psalm 124:3, 'they would have swallowed us alive'. The printed editions call the first sage Ḥanina; Kaufmann names him Ḥananya, like the sage after him. Kaufmann starts a new mishnah at Rabbi Ḥananya ben Teradyon; the printed editions keep both sayings in 3:2. In the Malachi verse a stray bet before סֵפֶר was erased.
sentences.say: רַבִּי חֲנַנְיָה סְגַן הַכֹּהֲנִים אוֹמֵר הֱוֵוי מִתְפַּלֵּל בִּשְׁלֹמָהּ שֶׁלַּמַּלְכוּת שֶׁאִילּוּלֵי מוֹרָאָה אִישׁ אֶת רְעֵהוּ חַיִּים בָּלַעְנוּ: רַבִּי חֲנַנְיָה בֶן תַּרְדְּיוֹן אוֹמֵר שְׁנַיִם שֶׁהָיוּ יוֹשְׁבִים וְאֵין בֵּינֵיהֶן דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה הֲרֵי זֶה מוֹשַׁב לֵיצִים שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וּבְמוֹשַׁב לֵיצִים לֹא יָשָׁב אֲבָל שְׁנַיִם שֶׁיּוֹשְׁבִים וַעֲסוּקִים בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה שְׁכִינָה בֵינֵיהֶם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר אָז נִדְבְּרוּ יִרְאֵי אֲדֹנָי אִישׁ אֶל רְעֵהוּ וַיַּקְשֵׁב אֲדֹנָי וַיּשְׁמַע וַיִּכָּתֵב סֵפֶר זִכָּרוֹן לְפָנָיו לְיִרְאֵי אֲדֹנָי וּלְחֹשְׁבֵי שְׁמוֹ

sentences.t: ר׳ שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵ׳ שְׁלֹשָׁה שֶׁאָכְלוּ עַל שׁוּלְחָן אֶחָד וְלֹא אָמְרוּ עָלָיו דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה הֲרֵי אֵילּוּ כְאֹכְלֵי זִבְחֵי מֵתִים שנ׳ כִּי כָל שׁוּלְחָנוֹת מַלְאוּ קִיא צוֹאָה בְלִי מָקוֹם אֲבַל שְׁלֹשׁ׳ שֶׁאָכְלוּ על שׁוּלְחָן אֶחָד וְאָמְרוּ עָלָיו דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְאִילּוּ אָכְלוּ מִשֻּׁלְחָנוּ שֶׁלְהַקָּבָּ״הֻ שנ׳ וַיְּדַבֵּר אֵלַיִ זֶה הַשֻּׁלְחָן אֲשֶׁר לִפְנֵי יָ׳י:
sentences.tr: Rabi Shimon omer: shlosha she-akhlu al shulḥan eḥad ve-lo amru alav divrei tora, harei elu ke-okhlei zivḥei metim, she-ne'emar: ki khol shulḥanot mal'u ki tso'a bli makom. Aval shlosha she-akhlu al shulḥan eḥad ve-amru alav divrei tora, ke-ilu akhlu mi-shulḥanu shel ha-Kadosh barukh hu, she-ne'emar: va-yedaber elay ze ha-shulḥan asher lifnei Adonay.
sentences.l: Rabbi Simeon says: three who ate at one table and did not say over it words of Torah, behold these are like eaters of sacrifices of the dead, as it is said: 'For all tables are full of vomit, filth, without place.' But three who ate at one table and said over it words of Torah, (it is) as-if they ate from the table of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said: 'And he spoke to me: this is the table that is before the LORD.'
sentences.i: Rabbi Simeon says: Three who have eaten at one table and spoken no words of Torah over it are as though they had eaten sacrifices to the dead, as it is said, 'For all the tables are covered with vomit and filth, and no place is left' (Isaiah 28:8). But three who have eaten at one table and spoken words of Torah over it are as though they had eaten from the table of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said, 'And he said to me, This is the table that stands before the LORD' (Ezekiel 41:22).
sentences.n: A plain 'Rabbi Simeon' in the Mishnah is Simeon bar Yoḥai, Akiva's student. 'Sacrifices of the dead' (Psalm 106:28) are offerings to idols. The first proof turns on a pun: מָקוֹם, 'place', is also a rabbinic name for God (see 3:10), so the sage hears Isaiah's בְּלִי מָקוֹם as 'without God'. In Ezekiel the table before the LORD is the altar: a meal with words of Torah becomes an offering. The printed editions read מִשֻּׁלְחָנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם, 'from the table of the Omnipresent'; Kaufmann has 'of the Holy One, blessed be He', and points the suffix -u (mi-shulḥanu). Kaufmann spells שׁוּלְחָן with a vav. A doubled וְלֹא was erased. Kaufmann marks no new mishnah here and runs this saying on from 3:2.
sentences.say: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר שְׁלֹשָׁה שֶׁאָכְלוּ עַל שׁוּלְחָן אֶחָד וְלֹא אָמְרוּ עָלָיו דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה הֲרֵי אֵילּוּ כְאֹכְלֵי זִבְחֵי מֵתִים שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר כִּי כָל שׁוּלְחָנוֹת מַלְאוּ קִיא צוֹאָה בְלִי מָקוֹם אֲבַל שְׁלֹשָׁה שֶׁאָכְלוּ על שׁוּלְחָן אֶחָד וְאָמְרוּ עָלָיו דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה כְאִילּוּ אָכְלוּ מִשֻּׁלְחָנוּ שֶׁל-הַקָּדוֹשׁ-בָּרוּךְ-הוּא שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וַיְּדַבֵּר אֵלַיִ זֶה הַשֻּׁלְחָן אֲשֶׁר לִפְנֵי אֲדֹנָי:

sentences.t: ר׳ חֲנַנְיָה בֶן חֲכִינַיִ אוֹמֵ׳ הַנֵּיעוֹר בַּלַּיְלָה וְהַמְהַלֵּךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ וּמַפְנֶה לִבּוֹ לְבַטָּלָה הֲרֵי זֶה מִתְחַיֵּיב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ:
sentences.tr: Rabi Ḥananya ben Ḥakhinay omer: ha-ne'or ba-layla, ve-ha-mehalekh ba-derekh, u-mafne libo le-vatala, harei ze mitḥayev be-nafsho.
sentences.l: Rabbi Ḥananya son of Ḥakhinai says: the one-who-stays-awake at night, and the one-who-walks on the road, and turns his heart to idleness, behold this one is-liable with his life.
sentences.i: Rabbi Ḥananya ben Ḥakhinai says: One who lies awake at night, or walks on the road, and turns his mind to idle things, forfeits his life.
sentences.n: מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ, 'becomes liable with his life', is the language of capital guilt. Night and the open road were dangerous places, and the hours spent there could go to words of Torah. The printed editions read וְהַמְהַלֵּךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ יְחִידִי, 'who walks on the road alone'; Kaufmann lacks יְחִידִי. The scribe left out the title; a second hand added ר׳. The printed editions call him Ḥanina.
sentences.say: רַבִּי חֲנַנְיָה בֶן חֲכִינַיִ אוֹמֵר הַנֵּיעוֹר בַּלַּיְלָה וְהַמְהַלֵּךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ וּמַפְנֶה לִבּוֹ לְבַטָּלָה הֲרֵי זֶה מִתְחַיֵּיב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ:

sentences.t: ר׳ נְחוֹנְיָה בֶן הַקָּנָה או׳ כָּל הַמְקַבֵּל עָלָיו עוֹל תּוֹרָה מַעֲבִירִים מִמֶּנּוּ עוֹל מַלְכוּת וְעוֹל דֶּרֶךְ הָאָרֶץ וְכֹל הַפּוֹרֵק מִמֶּנּוּ עוֹל תּוֹרָה נוֹתְנִים עָלָיו עוֹל מַלְכוּת וְעוֹל דֶּרֶךְ הָאָרֶץ:
sentences.tr: Rabi Neḥonya ben ha-Kana omer: kol ha-mekabel alav ol tora, ma'avirim mimenu ol malkhut ve-ol derekh ha-arets; ve-khol ha-porek mimenu ol tora, notnim alav ol malkhut ve-ol derekh ha-arets.
sentences.l: Rabbi Neḥunya son of Ha-Kana says: whoever receives upon himself the yoke of Torah, they remove from him the yoke of kingdom and the yoke of the way of the land; and whoever breaks-off from himself the yoke of Torah, they put upon him the yoke of kingdom and the yoke of the way of the land.
sentences.i: Rabbi Neḥunya ben Ha-Kana says: Whoever takes on the yoke of Torah is relieved of the yoke of government and the yoke of worldly cares; whoever throws off the yoke of Torah has the yoke of government and the yoke of worldly cares laid on him.
sentences.n: עוֹל מַלְכוּת, 'the yoke of the kingdom', is what the government imposes: taxes, forced labour, requisitions. עוֹל דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, 'the yoke of the way of the land', is the burden of earning a living. מַעֲבִירִים and נוֹתְנִים, 'they remove' and 'they put', are the Mishnah's impersonal plural; the unnamed 'they' is Heaven. In Kaufmann, עָלָיו is a second hand's writing over an erasure, and עוֹל before the first תּוֹרָה was added in the margin by a second hand. Kaufmann points the name Neḥonya.
sentences.say: רַבִּי נְחוֹנְיָה בֶן הַקָּנָה אוֹמֵר כָּל הַמְקַבֵּל עָלָיו עוֹל תּוֹרָה מַעֲבִירִים מִמֶּנּוּ עוֹל מַלְכוּת וְעוֹל דֶּרֶךְ הָאָרֶץ וְכֹל הַפּוֹרֵק מִמֶּנּוּ עוֹל תּוֹרָה נוֹתְנִים עָלָיו עוֹל מַלְכוּת וְעוֹל דֶּרֶךְ הָאָרֶץ:

sentences.t: ר׳ חֶלְפְּתָה אִישׁ כְּפַר חֲנַנְיָה אוֹ׳ עֲשָׂרָה שֶׁהָיוּ יוֹשְׁבִים וַעֲסוּקִים בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה שְׁכִינָה בֵינֵיהֶם שנ׳ אֱ׳הִים נִצָּב בַּעֲדַת אֵל מְנַיִן אֲפִילוּ חֲמִשָּׁה שנ׳ בְּקֶרֶב אֱלֹהִים יִשְׁפֹּט מְנַיִן אֲפִילּוּ שְׁלֹשָה שנ׳ וַאֲגוּדָּתוֹ עַל אֶרֶץ יְסָדָהּ מְנַיִן אֲפִילּוּ שְׁנַיִם שנ׳ אָז נִדְבְּרוּ יִרְאֵי יָ׳י אִישׁ אֶל רְעֵהוּ וַיַּקְשֵׁב יָ׳י וַיּשְׁמַע וַיִּכָּתֵב סֵפֶר זִכָּרוֹן לְפָנָיו לְיִרְאֵי יָ׳י וּלְחוֹשְׁבֵי שְׁמוֹ: מְנַיִן אֲפִילּוּ אֶחָד שנ׳ בְּכָל הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר אַזְכִּיר אֶת שְׁמִי אָבוֹא אֵלֶיךָ וּבֵרַכְתִּיךָ:
sentences.tr: Rabi Ḥelpeta ish Kfar Ḥananya omer: asara she-hayu yoshvim va-asukim be-divrei tora, shkhina beineihem, she-ne'emar: Elohim nitsav ba-adat El. Menayin afilu ḥamisha? She-ne'emar: be-kerev Elohim yishpot. Menayin afilu shlosha? She-ne'emar: va-agudato al erets yesadah. Menayin afilu shnayim? She-ne'emar: az nidberu yir'ei Adonay ish el re'ehu, va-yakshev Adonay va-yishma, va-yikatev sefer zikaron lefanav le-yir'ei Adonay u-le-ḥoshvei shmo. Menayin afilu eḥad? She-ne'emar: be-khol ha-makom asher azkir et shmi avo elekha u-verakhtikha.
sentences.l: Rabbi Ḥalafta man of Kefar Ḥananya says: ten who were sitting and occupied with words of Torah, the Presence is between them, as it is said: 'God stands in the congregation of God.' From-where (do we know) even five? As it is said: 'In the midst of judges He judges.' From-where even three? As it is said: 'And His bundle He founded on earth.' From-where even two? As it is said: 'Then those who fear the LORD spoke a man to his fellow, and the LORD listened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before Him for those who fear the LORD and for those who think on His name.' From-where even one? As it is said: 'In every place where I cause My name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you.'
sentences.i: Rabbi Ḥalafta of Kefar Ḥananya says: When ten sit and occupy themselves with words of Torah, the Divine Presence rests among them, as it is said, 'God stands in the divine assembly' (Psalm 82:1). How do we know this of even five? As it is said, 'He judges among the judges' (Psalm 82:1). Of even three? As it is said, 'He has founded His band upon the earth' (Amos 9:6). Of even two? As it is said, 'Then those who feared the LORD talked with one another; the LORD took note and listened, and a book of remembrance was written before Him for those who fear the LORD and give thought to His name' (Malachi 3:16). And of even one? As it is said, 'In every place where I cause My name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you' (Exodus 20:24).
sentences.n: Each number is drawn from a word in its verse. An עֵדָה, 'congregation', is ten, since the ten spies are called 'this evil congregation' (Numbers 14:27). The commentators explain the other two: a court of three judges is called אֱלֹהִים, and an אֲגוּדָּה, 'bundle', is what a hand of five fingers can hold. On that reasoning the printed editions pair five with Amos and three with the psalm; Kaufmann has them the other way round. The printed editions also call the sage Ḥalafta ben Dosa; Kaufmann has no 'ben Dosa' and points the name Ḥelpeta. The Malachi verse comes a second time here (see 3:2), and again a stray bet before סֵפֶר was erased. Exodus 20:24 is 20:21 in Hebrew Bibles.
sentences.say: רַבִּי חֶלְפְּתָה אִישׁ כְּפַר חֲנַנְיָה אוֹמֵר עֲשָׂרָה שֶׁהָיוּ יוֹשְׁבִים וַעֲסוּקִים בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה שְׁכִינָה בֵינֵיהֶם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר אֱלֹהִים נִצָּב בַּעֲדַת אֵל מְנַיִן אֲפִילוּ חֲמִשָּׁה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּקֶרֶב אֱלֹהִים יִשְׁפֹּט מְנַיִן אֲפִילּוּ שְׁלֹשָה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וַאֲגוּדָּתוֹ עַל אֶרֶץ יְסָדָהּ מְנַיִן אֲפִילּוּ שְׁנַיִם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר אָז נִדְבְּרוּ יִרְאֵי אֲדֹנָי אִישׁ אֶל רְעֵהוּ וַיַּקְשֵׁב אֲדֹנָי וַיּשְׁמַע וַיִּכָּתֵב סֵפֶר זִכָּרוֹן לְפָנָיו לְיִרְאֵי אֲדֹנָי וּלְחוֹשְׁבֵי שְׁמוֹ: מְנַיִן אֲפִילּוּ אֶחָד שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּכָל הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר אַזְכִּיר אֶת שְׁמִי אָבוֹא אֵלֶיךָ וּבֵרַכְתִּיךָ:

sentences.t: ר׳ אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן יְהוּדָה אִישׁ בִּרְתוֹתָה אוֹ׳ תֶּן לוֹ מִשֶּׁלּוֹ שֶׁאַתְּ וְשֶׁלָּךְ שֶׁלּוֹ וְכֵן הוּא אוֹ׳ בְּדָוִד כִּי מִמְּךָ הַכֹּל מִיָּדְךָ נָתַנּוּ לָךְ: ר׳ יַעֲקֹב אוֹ׳ הַמְהַלֵּךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ וְשׁוֹנֶה וּמַפְסִיק מִשְׁנָתוֹ וְאוֹ׳ מַה נָּאֶה אִילָן זֶה וּמַה נָּאֶה נִיר זֶה מַעֲלִין עָלָיו כְּאִילּוּ מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ:
sentences.tr: Rabi Elazar ben Yehuda ish Birtota omer: ten lo mi-shelo, she-at ve-shelakh shelo. Ve-khen hu omer be-David: ki mimkha ha-kol, mi-yadkha natanu lakh. Rabi Ya'akov omer: ha-mehalekh ba-derekh ve-shone, u-mafsik mishnato ve-omer: ma na'e ilan ze, u-ma na'e nir ze, ma'alin alav ke-ilu mitḥayev be-nafsho.
sentences.l: Rabbi Elazar son of Judah man of Bartota says: give to Him from what-is-His, for you and what-is-yours are His. And so it says about David: 'For from You is everything, from Your hand we have given to You.' Rabbi Jacob says: one-who-walks on the road and is reciting, and breaks-off his recitation and says: how lovely is this tree, and how lovely is this ploughed-field, they reckon it to him as-if he is-liable with his life.
sentences.i: Rabbi Elazar ben Judah of Bartota says: Give Him what is His, for you and all you have are His. So David says, 'For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You' (1 Chronicles 29:14). Rabbi Jacob says: One who is walking on the road going over his learning, and breaks off to say, 'How lovely this tree is! How lovely this field is!' is regarded as though he had forfeited his life.
sentences.n: שׁוֹנֶה, 'repeating', is how study was done: learning meant reciting memorized texts aloud, and מִשְׁנָה is the thing so recited. נִיר is a freshly ploughed field. מַעֲלִין עָלָיו, 'they bring it up against him', means 'he is regarded'; the printed editions read מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב, 'Scripture regards him'. Kaufmann's שֶׁאַתְּ uses the Mishnaic אַתְּ, 'you', which serves for a man too; the printed text has שֶׁאַתָּה. The printed editions name the first sage Elazar of Bartota, without 'ben Judah'. The verse in Chronicles reads וּמִיָּדְךָ; here its vav was erased, and כֵן is a second hand's writing over an erasure. Kaufmann starts a new mishnah at Rabbi Jacob; the printed editions keep both sayings in 3:7.
sentences.say: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן יְהוּדָה אִישׁ בִּרְתוֹתָה אוֹמֵר תֶּן לוֹ מִשֶּׁלּוֹ שֶׁאַתְּ וְשֶׁלָּךְ שֶׁלּוֹ וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר בְּדָוִד כִּי מִמְּךָ הַכֹּל מִיָּדְךָ נָתַנּוּ לָךְ: רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר הַמְהַלֵּךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ וְשׁוֹנֶה וּמַפְסִיק מִשְׁנָתוֹ וְאוֹמֵר מַה נָּאֶה אִילָן זֶה וּמַה נָּאֶה נִיר זֶה מַעֲלִין עָלָיו כְּאִילּוּ מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ:

sentences.t: ר׳ דוֹסְתִּי בִרְ׳ יַנַּיִי אוֹמֵ׳ מִשֵּׁם ר׳ מֵאִיר כָּל הַשָׁכַח דָּבָר אֶחָד מִמִּשְׁנָתוֹ מַעְלִין עָלָיו כְּאִילּוּ מִתְחַיֵּיב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שנ׳ רַק הִשָּׁמֵר לְךָ וּשְׁמֹר נַפְשְׁךָ מְאֹד פֶּן תִּשְׁכַּח אֶת הַדְּבָרִים אֲשֶׁר רָאוּ עֵינֶיךָ יָכוֹל אֲפִילּוּ תַקְפָה עָלָיו מִשְׁנָתוֹ תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַ׳ וּפֶן יָסוּרוּ מִלְבָבְךָ כָּל יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ הָא אֵינוּ מִתְחַיֵּיב עַד שֶׁיֵּשֶׁב לוֹ וִיסִירֵם מִלִּבּוֹ:
sentences.tr: Rabi Dosti birabi Yanay omer mi-shem Rabi Me'ir: kol ha-shakhaḥ davar eḥad mi-mishnato, ma'lin alav ke-ilu mitḥayev be-nafsho, she-ne'emar: rak hishamer lekha u-shmor nafshekha me'od pen tishkaḥ et ha-dvarim asher ra'u eineikha. Yakhol afilu takfa alav mishnato? Talmud lomar: u-fen yasuru mi-levavkha kol yemei ḥayekha. Ha, einu mitḥayev ad she-yeshev lo vi-sirem mi-libo.
sentences.l: Rabbi Dostai son-of-Rabbi Yannai says in the name of Rabbi Meir: whoever has-forgotten one thing of his learning, they reckon it to him as-if he is-liable with his life, as it is said: 'Only take-care for-yourself and guard your soul greatly, lest you forget the things that your eyes saw.' Could-it-be even (if) his learning overpowered him? Teaching to-say: 'and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life.' So, he is not liable until he sits and removes them from his heart.
sentences.i: Rabbi Dostai ben Rabbi Yannai says in the name of Rabbi Meir: Whoever forgets a single thing of his learning is regarded as though he had forfeited his life, as it is said, 'Only be on your guard and watch yourself closely, so that you do not forget the things your eyes have seen' (Deuteronomy 4:9). Might that hold even when his learning proved too hard for him? The verse goes on to say, 'and so that they do not slip from your heart all the days of your life.' So he is liable only when he sits down and puts them out of his mind.
sentences.n: יָכוֹל … תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר, 'one might think … the teaching says', is the standard move of rabbinic midrash: propose a reading, then rule it out from the wording of the verse. Here the second half of Deuteronomy 4:9 limits the first: forgetting counts against a person when he lets his learning go by choice. תָּקְפָה עָלָיו, 'overpowered him', means the material was too hard to retain. הָא, 'so, hence', is Aramaic. הַשָּׁכַח joins the article to a perfect verb, 'who has forgotten', where the printed text has the participle הַשּׁוֹכֵחַ. אֵינוּ is Kaufmann's spelling of אֵינוֹ. בִרְ׳ abbreviates בְּרַבִּי, 'son of Rabbi'; Kaufmann points the sage's name Dosti. In the first מִמִּשְׁנָתוֹ the second mem is a second hand's writing over an erasure; a stray mem before the second מִשְׁנָתוֹ was erased.
sentences.say: רַבִּי דוֹסְתִּי בְּרַבִּי יַנַּיִי אוֹמֵר מִשֵּׁם רַבִּי מֵאִיר כָּל הַשָׁכַח דָּבָר אֶחָד מִמִּשְׁנָתוֹ מַעְלִין עָלָיו כְּאִילּוּ מִתְחַיֵּיב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר רַק הִשָּׁמֵר לְךָ וּשְׁמֹר נַפְשְׁךָ מְאֹד פֶּן תִּשְׁכַּח אֶת הַדְּבָרִים אֲשֶׁר רָאוּ עֵינֶיךָ יָכוֹל אֲפִילּוּ תַקְפָה עָלָיו מִשְׁנָתוֹ תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר וּפֶן יָסוּרוּ מִלְבָבְךָ כָּל יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ הָא אֵינוּ מִתְחַיֵּיב עַד שֶׁיֵּשֶׁב לוֹ וִיסִירֵם מִלִּבּוֹ:

sentences.t: ר׳ חֲנִינָה בֶן דּוֹסָה אוֹמֵ׳ כָּל שֶׁיִּרְאַת חֶטְאוֹ קוֹדֶמֶת לְחָכְמָתוֹ חָכְמָתוֹ מִתְקַיֶּימֶת חָכְמָתוֹ קוֹדֶמֶת לְיִרְאַת חֶטְאוֹ אֵין חָוכְמָתוֹ מִתְקַיֶּימֶת: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵ׳ כָּל שֶׁמַּעֲשָׂיו מְרוּבִּים מֵחָכְמָתוֹ חָוכְמָתוֹ מִתְקַיֶּימֶת חָוכְמָתוֹ מְרוּבָּה מִמַּעֲשָׂיו אֵין חָכְמָתוֹ מִתְקַיֶּימֶת
sentences.tr: Rabi Ḥanina ben Dosa omer: kol she-yir'at ḥet'o kodemet le-ḥokhmato, ḥokhmato mitkayemet; ḥokhmato kodemet le-yir'at ḥet'o, ein ḥokhmato mitkayemet. Hu haya omer: kol she-ma'asav merubim me-ḥokhmato, ḥokhmato mitkayemet; ḥokhmato meruba mi-ma'asav, ein ḥokhmato mitkayemet.
sentences.l: Rabbi Ḥanina son of Dosa says: anyone whose fear of his sin comes-before his wisdom, his wisdom endures; his wisdom comes-before his fear of his sin, his wisdom does not endure. He was saying: anyone whose deeds are more than his wisdom, his wisdom endures; his wisdom is more than his deeds, his wisdom does not endure.
sentences.i: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa says: When a man's fear of sin comes before his wisdom, his wisdom will last; when his wisdom comes before his fear of sin, his wisdom will not last. He used to say: When a man's deeds exceed his wisdom, his wisdom will last; when his wisdom exceeds his deeds, his wisdom will not last.
sentences.n: Ḥanina ben Dosa was a Galilean holy man of the first century, remembered for prayers that healed the sick. יִרְאַת חֵטְא, 'fear of sin', is the dread of doing wrong. מִתְקַיֶּימֶת, 'endures', is a Hitpael of קוּם, 'stand'. The scribe spelled חָכְמָה with a vav for the short o (חוכמה); a later hand erased most of these vavs and missed a few, so both spellings stand in the text. אוֹמֵר after the name and קוֹדֶמֶת in the second clause were added in the margin. Kaufmann starts a new mishnah at 'He used to say'; the printed editions keep both sayings in 3:9.
sentences.say: רַבִּי חֲנִינָה בֶן דּוֹסָה אוֹמֵר כָּל שֶׁיִּרְאַת חֶטְאוֹ קוֹדֶמֶת לְחָכְמָתוֹ חָכְמָתוֹ מִתְקַיֶּימֶת חָכְמָתוֹ קוֹדֶמֶת לְיִרְאַת חֶטְאוֹ אֵין חָוכְמָתוֹ מִתְקַיֶּימֶת: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר כָּל שֶׁמַּעֲשָׂיו מְרוּבִּים מֵחָכְמָתוֹ חָוכְמָתוֹ מִתְקַיֶּימֶת חָוכְמָתוֹ מְרוּבָּה מִמַּעֲשָׂיו אֵין חָכְמָתוֹ מִתְקַיֶּימֶת

sentences.t: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵ׳ כָּל שֶׁרוּחַ הַבְּרִיוֹת נוֹחָה מִמֶּנּוּ רוּחַ הַמָּקוֹם נוֹחָה מִמֶּנּוּ וְכָל שֶׁאֵין רוּחַ הַבְּרִיּוֹת נוֹחָה הֵימֶנּוּ אֵין רוּחַ הַמָּקוֹם נוֹחָה מִמֶּנּוּ ר׳ דוֹסָה בֶן הַרְכִינָס אוֹ׳ שְׁנַת שַׁחְרִית וְיֵין צָהֳרַיִם וְשִׂיחַת הַיְלָדִים וִישִׁיבַת כְּנֵסָיוֹת שֶׁלְעַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ מוֹצִיאִין אֶת הָאָדָם מִן הָעוֹלָם:
sentences.tr: Hu haya omer: kol she-ruaḥ ha-briyot noḥa mimenu, ruaḥ ha-makom noḥa mimenu; ve-khol she-ein ruaḥ ha-briyot noḥa heimenu, ein ruaḥ ha-makom noḥa mimenu. Rabi Dosa ben Harkinas omer: shnat shaḥrit, ve-yein tsohorayim, ve-siḥat ha-yeladim, vi-shivat knesayot shel amei ha-arets motsi'in et ha-adam min ha-olam.
sentences.l: He was saying: anyone with whom the spirit of people is pleased, the spirit of the Omnipresent is pleased with him; and anyone with whom the spirit of people is not pleased, the spirit of the Omnipresent is not pleased with him. Rabbi Dosa son of Harkinas says: sleep of morning, and wine of noon, and chatter of the children, and sitting of assemblies of the people of the land take the person out of the world.
sentences.i: He used to say: One whom people are pleased with, the Omnipresent is pleased with; one whom people are not pleased with, the Omnipresent is not pleased with. Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas says: Late-morning sleep, midday wine, children's chatter, and sitting in the gatherings of the ignorant drive a person out of the world.
sentences.n: רוּחַ … נוֹחָה מִמֶּנּוּ, 'the spirit is at ease from him', means 'is pleased with him'. הַמָּקוֹם, literally 'the Place', is a rabbinic name for God; we render it 'the Omnipresent'. עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ, 'people of the land', are in rabbinic usage the unlearned, careless about tithes and purity. 'Drive a person out of the world': these habits waste the life he has. The second clause of the first saying (from וְכָל שֶׁאֵין to הֵימֶנּוּ) was added in the margin. Kaufmann gives Dosa's list in construct forms, שְׁנַת שַׁחְרִית and יֵין צָהֳרַיִם; the scribe first wrote שֶׁל before both second words and then erased it. The printed text reads שֵׁנָה שֶׁל שַׁחֲרִית וְיַיִן שֶׁל צָהֳרַיִם, and וִישִׁיבַת בָּתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת, 'sitting in the meeting houses'. Kaufmann starts a new mishnah at Rabbi Dosa; the printed editions keep it in 3:10.
sentences.say: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר כָּל שֶׁרוּחַ הַבְּרִיוֹת נוֹחָה מִמֶּנּוּ רוּחַ הַמָּקוֹם נוֹחָה מִמֶּנּוּ וְכָל שֶׁאֵין רוּחַ הַבְּרִיּוֹת נוֹחָה הֵימֶנּוּ אֵין רוּחַ הַמָּקוֹם נוֹחָה מִמֶּנּוּ רַבִּי דוֹסָה בֶן הַרְכִינָס אוֹמֵר שְׁנַת שַׁחְרִית וְיֵין צָהֳרַיִם וְשִׂיחַת הַיְלָדִים וִישִׁיבַת כְּנֵסָיוֹת שֶׁלְעַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ מוֹצִיאִין אֶת הָאָדָם מִן הָעוֹלָם:

sentences.t: ר׳ אֶלְעָזָר הַמּוּדָעִי אוֹ׳ הַמְחַלֵּל אֶת הַקָּדָשִׁים וְהַמְבַזֶּה אֶת הַמּוֹעֲדוֹת וְהַמְגַלֶּה פָנִים בַּתּוֹרָה וְהַמֵּפֵר בְּרִיתוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ וְהַמְּאַדִּים אֶת פְּנֵי חֲבֵירוֹ אַפְ עַל פִּי שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּיָדוֹ מַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים אֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא:
sentences.tr: Rabi Elazar ha-Muda'i omer: ha-meḥalel et ha-kodashim, ve-ha-mevaze et ha-mo'adot, ve-ha-megale fanim ba-tora, ve-ha-mefer brito shel Avraham avinu, ve-ha-me'adim et pnei ḥavero, af al pi she-yesh be-yado ma'asim tovim, ein lo ḥelek la-olam ha-ba.
sentences.l: Rabbi Elazar the Modiite says: one-who-profanes the holy-things, and one-who-despises the festivals, and one-who-uncovers face in the Torah, and one-who-annuls his covenant of Abraham our father, and one-who-makes-red the face of his fellow, even though there are good deeds in his hand, he has no share in the world to come.
sentences.i: Rabbi Elazar of Modi'in says: One who profanes sacred offerings, treats the festivals with contempt, defies the Torah brazenly, undoes the covenant of Abraham our father, or shames his fellow to his face — even if he has good deeds to his credit, he has no share in the world to come.
sentences.n: הַקָּדָשִׁים are sacrificial offerings and other property dedicated to the Temple. הַמּוֹעֲדוֹת are the festivals, above all their intermediate days, when work was partly allowed. 'Uncovering the face' toward the Torah is brazen defiance of it. 'Annulling the covenant of Abraham' means undoing circumcision: some Jews under Greek and Roman rule had the foreskin surgically restored so they could appear naked in the gymnasium. Kaufmann has הַמְּאַדִּים, 'who makes red', where the printed text has הַמַּלְבִּין, 'who makes white'; both picture public shaming, one by the blush and the other by the blood draining from the face. Kaufmann's list is shorter and in a different order. The printed text reads הַמַּלְבִּין פְּנֵי חֲבֵרוֹ בָּרַבִּים, 'in public', and הַמְגַלֶּה פָנִים בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁלֹּא כַהֲלָכָה, 'interpreting the Torah against the law', and gives the sinner תּוֹרָה וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים, 'Torah and good deeds'. Kaufmann points the sage's town-name ha-Muda'i.
sentences.say: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר הַמּוּדָעִי אוֹמֵר הַמְחַלֵּל אֶת הַקָּדָשִׁים וְהַמְבַזֶּה אֶת הַמּוֹעֲדוֹת וְהַמְגַלֶּה פָנִים בַּתּוֹרָה וְהַמֵּפֵר בְּרִיתוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ וְהַמְּאַדִּים אֶת פְּנֵי חֲבֵירוֹ אַפְ עַל פִּי שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּיָדוֹ מַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים אֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא:

sentences.t: ר׳ יִשְׁמָעֵא׳ אוֹמ׳ הֱוֵוי קַל רֹאש וְנוֹחַ תִּישְׁחוֹרֶת וֶהֱוֵוי מְקַבֵּל אֶת כָּל הָאָדָם בְּשִׂמְחָה:
sentences.tr: Rabi Yishma'el omer: hevei kal rosh ve-noaḥ tishḥoret, ve-hevei mekabel et kol ha-adam be-simḥa.
sentences.l: Rabbi Ishmael says: be light (of) head and easy (to) youth, and be receiving every person with joy.
sentences.i: Rabbi Ishmael says: Be quick to serve a superior and easy with the young, and receive everyone with gladness.
sentences.n: The first half is a famous puzzle, and every rendering of it is a guess. One common reading: רֹאשׁ, 'head', is a superior, and תִּשְׁחוֹרֶת, from שָׁחוֹר, 'black', is a young man with black hair (Ecclesiastes 11:10 pairs שַׁחֲרוּת with youth). So: be quick to serve your elders and easy with the young. Other readings take תִּשְׁחוֹרֶת as the authorities or as forced service. קַל רֹאשׁ here means readiness; it differs from קַלּוּת רֹאשׁ, 'levity', in the next mishnah. The printed text has קַל לְרֹאשׁ וְנוֹחַ לְתִשְׁחֹרֶת, with 'to' twice; Kaufmann has no lamed in either place. The shin of רֹאש lacks its dot.
sentences.say: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל אוֹמֵר הֱוֵוי קַל רֹאש וְנוֹחַ תִּישְׁחוֹרֶת וֶהֱוֵוי מְקַבֵּל אֶת כָּל הָאָדָם בְּשִׂמְחָה:

sentences.t: ר׳ עֲקִיבָה אוֹ׳ שְׂחוֹק וְקַלּוּת רֹאשׁ מַרְגִּילִים אֶת הָאָדָם לָעֶרְיָה מַעַשְׂרוֹת סְיַיג לַתּוֹרָה נְדָרִים סְיַיג לִפְרִישׁוּת סְיַיג לַחָכְמָה שְׁתִיקָה:
sentences.tr: Rabi Akiva omer: sḥok ve-kalut rosh margilim et ha-adam la-erya. Ma'asrot siyag la-tora; nedarim siyag li-frishut; siyag la-ḥokhma shtika.
sentences.l: Rabbi Akiva says: laughter and lightness of head accustom the person to lewdness. Tithes (are) a fence for the Torah; vows a fence for abstinence; a fence for wisdom: silence.
sentences.i: Rabbi Akiva says: Jesting and levity lead a person on to sexual sin. Tithes are a fence around the Torah; vows are a fence around self-restraint; the fence around wisdom is silence.
sentences.n: עֶרְוָה (Kaufmann spells it עֶרְיָה) is literally 'nakedness', the rabbinic term for forbidden sexual relations. סְיָג, 'fence', is the image from 1:1: a safeguard set around something precious. The printed text has four fences: מָסֹרֶת סְיָג לַתּוֹרָה, 'tradition is a fence for the Torah', then מַעַשְׂרוֹת סְיָג לָעֹשֶׁר, 'tithes are a fence for wealth'. Kaufmann has three and pairs tithes with the Torah, either through a slip in copying or from a different text. The last clause turns the order round to end on 'silence'. אֶת הָאָדָם was added in the margin.
sentences.say: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָה אוֹמֵר שְׂחוֹק וְקַלּוּת רֹאשׁ מַרְגִּילִים אֶת הָאָדָם לָעֶרְיָה מַעַשְׂרוֹת סְיַיג לַתּוֹרָה נְדָרִים סְיַיג לִפְרִישׁוּת סְיַיג לַחָכְמָה שְׁתִיקָה:

sentences.t: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵ׳ חָבִיב אָדָם שֶׁנִּבְרָא בְצֶלֶם חִיבָּה יְתֵירָה נוֹדַעַת לוֹ שֶׁנִּיבְרָא בְצֶלֶם אֱ׳הִים שנ׳ כִּי בְצֶלֶם אֱ׳הִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם חֲבִיבִים יִשְׂרָאֵ׳ שֶׁנִּיקְרְאוּ בָנִים חִיבָּה יְתֵירָה נוֹדַעַת לָהֶם שֶׁנִּיקְרְאוּ בָנִים לַמָּקוֹם בָּנִים אַתֶּם לְיָ׳י אֱ׳הֵיכֶם חֲבִיבִים יִשְׂרָאֵ׳ שֶׁנִּיתַּן לָהֶם כֶּלִי שֶׁבּוֹ נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם חִיבָּה יְתֵירָה נוֹדַעַת לָהֶם שֶׁנִּיתַּן לָהֶם כֶּלִי שֶׁבּוֹ נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם שנ׳ כִּי לֶקַח טוֹב נָתַתִּי לָכֶם תּוֹרַתִי אַל תַּעַזֹבוּ
sentences.tr: Hu haya omer: ḥaviv adam she-nivra be-tselem; ḥiba yetera noda'at lo she-nivra be-tselem Elohim, she-ne'emar: ki be-tselem Elohim asa et ha-adam. Ḥavivim Yisra'el she-nikre'u vanim; ḥiba yetera noda'at lahem she-nikre'u vanim la-makom: banim atem la-Adonay Eloheikhem. Ḥavivim Yisra'el she-nitan lahem keli she-bo nivra ha-olam; ḥiba yetera noda'at lahem she-nitan lahem keli she-bo nivra ha-olam, she-ne'emar: ki lekaḥ tov natati lakhem, torati al ta'azovu.
sentences.l: He was saying: beloved is man, that he was created in an image; an extra love is made-known to him, that he was created in the image of God, as it is said: 'for in the image of God He made the man.' Beloved are Israel, that they were called children; an extra love is made-known to them, that they were called children to the Omnipresent: 'Children you are to the LORD your God.' Beloved are Israel, that there was given to them an instrument with which the world was created; an extra love is made-known to them, that there was given to them an instrument with which the world was created, as it is said: 'For good teaching I have given to you; my Torah do not forsake.'
sentences.i: He used to say: Beloved is humankind, for they were created in the image; it is a further mark of love that they were told they were created in the image of God, as it is said, 'For in the image of God He made humankind' (Genesis 9:6). Beloved are Israel, for they are called children; it is a further mark of love that they were told they are called children of the Omnipresent: 'You are children of the LORD your God' (Deuteronomy 14:1). Beloved are Israel, for they were given the instrument with which the world was created; it is a further mark of love that they were told they were given the instrument with which the world was created, as it is said, 'For I have given you good teaching; do not forsake My Torah' (Proverbs 4:2).
sentences.n: חִבָּה יְתֵירָה נוֹדַעַת לוֹ, 'an extra love made known to him': being loved is one gift, and being told of it is a second. The instrument is the Torah, which rabbinic tradition pictures as the plan God followed in creating the world. All three proof-texts stand in Kaufmann's margin; the second has no שנ׳ before it. The printed text calls the Torah כְּלִי חֶמְדָּה, 'a precious instrument'; Kaufmann has plain כֶּלִי. In the first שֶׁנִּבְרָא the nun was written above the line, and a doubled שֶׁנִּיתַּן was erased. Kaufmann marks no new mishnah after this saying: 'All is foreseen' (3:15) runs straight on. Vowel points supplied by the editor where the manuscript leaves a letter bare: שֶׁנִּיבְרָא.
sentences.say: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר חָבִיב אָדָם שֶׁנִּבְרָא בְצֶלֶם חִיבָּה יְתֵירָה נוֹדַעַת לוֹ שֶׁנִּיבְרָא בְצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר כִּי בְצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם חֲבִיבִים יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנִּיקְרְאוּ בָנִים חִיבָּה יְתֵירָה נוֹדַעַת לָהֶם שֶׁנִּיקְרְאוּ בָנִים לַמָּקוֹם בָּנִים אַתֶּם לַאדֹנָי אֱלֹהֵיכֶם חֲבִיבִים יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנִּיתַּן לָהֶם כֶּלִי שֶׁבּוֹ נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם חִיבָּה יְתֵירָה נוֹדַעַת לָהֶם שֶׁנִּיתַּן לָהֶם כֶּלִי שֶׁבּוֹ נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר כִּי לֶקַח טוֹב נָתַתִּי לָכֶם תּוֹרַתִי אַל תַּעַזֹבוּ

sentences.t: הַכֹּל צָפוּי וְהָרְשׁוּת נְתוּנָה וּבְטוּב הָעוֹלָם נִידוֹן וְהַכֹּל לְפִי רוֹב הַמַּעֲשֶׂה:
sentences.tr: Ha-kol tsafuy, ve-ha-rshut ntuna, u-ve-tuv ha-olam nidon, ve-ha-kol lefi rov ha-ma'ase.
sentences.l: Everything is foreseen, and the permission is given; and with goodness the world is judged; and everything (is) according to the majority of the deed.
sentences.i: All is foreseen, yet freedom of choice is given. The world is judged with goodness, and everything goes by the greater part of one's deeds.
sentences.n: Kaufmann writes this straight on from 3:14 with no break, so it continues Rabbi Akiva's sayings; the printed editions give it its own number. God sees everything in advance, and people still choose: the Mishnah states both and stops there. רְשׁוּת, 'authority' in 1:10, here means permission, the freedom to choose. רוֹב הַמַּעֲשֶׂה is read either as 'the majority of one's deeds', good outweighing bad, or as 'the number of good acts', many small ones counting for more than one large one. The kaf of the second וְהַכֹּל lacks its vowel point. Vowel points supplied by the editor where the manuscript leaves a letter bare: וְהַכֹּל.

sentences.t: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמ׳ הַכֹּל נָתוּן בַּעֲרָבִים וּמְצוּדָה פְּרוּשָׂה אל כָּל הַחַיִּים הֶחָנוּת פְּתוּחָה וְהַחַנְוָונִי מַקִּיף הַפִּינְקֵס פְּתוּחָה וְהַיָּד כּוֹתֶבֶת וְהַגַּבָּאִים מְחַזְרִים תָּמִיד בְּכָל יוֹם וְנִפְרָעִין מִן הָאָדָם לְדַעְתּוֹ: וְשֶׁלֹּא לְדַעְתּוֹ וְהַדִּין דִּין אֱמֶת וְהַכֹּל מְתוּקָּן לִסְעוֹדָה:
sentences.tr: Hu haya omer: ha-kol natun ba-aravim, u-metsuda prusa al kol ha-ḥayim. He-ḥanut ptuḥa, ve-ha-ḥanvani makif; ha-pinkes ptuḥa, ve-ha-yad kotevet; ve-ha-gaba'im meḥazrim tamid be-khol yom, ve-nifra'in min ha-adam le-da'to ve-she-lo le-da'to; ve-ha-din din emet, ve-ha-kol metukan li-s'uda.
sentences.l: He was saying: everything is given on pledges, and a net is spread over all the living. The shop is open, and the shopkeeper gives-credit; the ledger is open, and the hand writes; and the collectors go-round continually every day, and exact-payment from the person with his knowledge and without his knowledge; and the judgment is a judgment of truth, and everything is prepared for the feast.
sentences.i: He used to say: Everything is given on pledge, and a net is spread over all the living. The shop is open, and the shopkeeper sells on credit; the ledger lies open, and the hand writes. The collectors make their rounds every day and take payment from a person whether he knows it or not. The judgment is a true judgment, and everything is made ready for the banquet.
sentences.n: One extended picture of life as goods bought on credit. In the usual reading the shopkeeper is God, the ledger records every debt, the collectors are the troubles that exact payment whether a person sees the reason or not, and the banquet is the reward of the world to come. פִּנְקֵס, 'ledger', is a Greek loanword (pinax, writing tablet); Kaufmann makes it feminine (פְּתוּחָה). Kaufmann has בַּעֲרָבִים, 'on pledges', where the printed text has בְּעֵרָבוֹן, 'on pledge', and it lacks two clauses of the printed text: וְכָל הָרוֹצֶה לִלְווֹת יָבוֹא וְיִלְוֶה, 'whoever wants to borrow may come and borrow', and וְיֵשׁ לָהֶם עַל מַה שֶׁיִּסְמֹכוּ, 'and they have something to rely on'. The unpointed אל stands for עַל, 'over', probably Kaufmann's alef-for-ayin spelling. מִן was added in the margin, the he of הָאָדָם is a second hand's writing over an erasure, and a yod was erased from מְחַזְרִים. The scribe's colon after the first לְדַעְתּוֹ falls in mid-sentence.
sentences.say: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר הַכֹּל נָתוּן בַּעֲרָבִים וּמְצוּדָה פְּרוּשָׂה אל כָּל הַחַיִּים הֶחָנוּת פְּתוּחָה וְהַחַנְוָונִי מַקִּיף הַפִּינְקֵס פְּתוּחָה וְהַיָּד כּוֹתֶבֶת וְהַגַּבָּאִים מְחַזְרִים תָּמִיד בְּכָל יוֹם וְנִפְרָעִין מִן הָאָדָם לְדַעְתּוֹ: וְשֶׁלֹּא לְדַעְתּוֹ וְהַדִּין דִּין אֱמֶת וְהַכֹּל מְתוּקָּן לִסְעוֹדָה:

sentences.t: ר׳ אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה אוֹ׳ אִם אֵין תּוֹרָה אֵין דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ אִם אֵין דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ אֵין תּוֹרָה אִם אֵין חָכְמָה אֵין יִרְאָה אִם אֵין יִרְאָה אֵין חָכְמָה אִם אֵין דַעַת אֵין בִּינָה אִם אֵין בִּינָה אֵין דַּעַת אִם אֵין קֶמַח אֵין תּוֹרָה אִם אֵין תּוֹרָה אֵין קֶמַח הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵ׳ כָּל שֶׁחָכְמָתוֹ מְרוּבָּה מִמַּעֲשָׂיו לְמָה הוּא דוֹמֶה לְאִילָן שֶׁנּוֹפוֹ מרובה וְשָׁרָשָׁיו מְעוּטִין וְהָרוּחַ בָּאת וְעוֹקְרַתּוּ וְהָפְכַתּוּ עַל פָּנָיו וְכָל שֶׁמַּעֲשָׂיו מְרוּבִּין מֵחָכְמָתוֹ לְמָה הוּא דוֹמֶה לְאִילָן שֶׁנּוֹפוֹ מְמוּעָט וְשָׁרָשָׁיו מְרוּבִּים אֲפִילּוּ כָל הָרוּחוֹת בָּאוֹת עָלָיו אֵין מְזִיזוֹת אוֹתוֹ מִמְּקוֹמוֹ
sentences.tr: Rabi Elazar ben Azarya omer: im ein tora ein derekh erets; im ein derekh erets ein tora. Im ein ḥokhma ein yir'a; im ein yir'a ein ḥokhma. Im ein da'at ein bina; im ein bina ein da'at. Im ein kemaḥ ein tora; im ein tora ein kemaḥ. Hu haya omer: kol she-ḥokhmato meruba mi-ma'asav, le-ma hu dome? Le-ilan she-nofo meruba ve-sharashav me'utin, ve-ha-ruaḥ ba'at ve-okratu ve-hofkhatu al panav. Ve-khol she-ma'asav merubin me-ḥokhmato, le-ma hu dome? Le-ilan she-nofo memu'at ve-sharashav merubim; afilu kol ha-ruḥot ba'ot alav, ein mezizot oto mi-mkomo.
sentences.l: Rabbi Elazar son of Azarya says: if there is no Torah, there is no way of the land; if there is no way of the land, there is no Torah. If there is no wisdom, there is no fear; if there is no fear, there is no wisdom. If there is no knowledge, there is no understanding; if there is no understanding, there is no knowledge. If there is no flour, there is no Torah; if there is no Torah, there is no flour. He was saying: anyone whose wisdom is more than his deeds, to what is he like? To a tree whose foliage is much and its roots few, and the wind comes and uproots-it and overturns-it on its face. And anyone whose deeds are more than his wisdom, to what is he like? To a tree whose foliage is little and its roots many: even (if) all the winds come upon it, they do not move it from its place.
sentences.i: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says: Without Torah there is no decent conduct; without decent conduct there is no Torah. Without wisdom there is no fear of God; without fear of God there is no wisdom. Without knowledge there is no understanding; without understanding there is no knowledge. Without bread there is no Torah; without Torah there is no bread. He used to say: One whose wisdom exceeds his deeds — what is he like? A tree with abundant foliage and few roots: the wind comes, tears it up and throws it flat on its face. But one whose deeds exceed his wisdom — what is he like? A tree with little foliage and many roots: even if all the winds come and blow against it, they cannot move it from its place.
sentences.n: דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, 'the way of the land', covers both decent conduct and earning a living; קֶמַח, 'flour', is bread on the table. לְמָה הוּא דוֹמֶה, 'to what is he like?', opens a rabbinic parable (mashal). עוֹקְרַתּוּ and הָפְכַתּוּ are feminine participles with the suffix 'it' (רוּחַ, 'wind', is feminine), in Kaufmann's form -attu; בָּאת is a short spelling of בָּאָה, 'comes'. The printed text speaks of the tree's branches, עֲנָפָיו, and adds a verse to each tree (Jeremiah 17:6 and 17:8); Kaufmann has נוֹפוֹ, 'its foliage', and no verses. Corrections: the scribe began כָּל שֶׁמַּעֲשָׂיו in the wrong place and erased it; the unpointed מרובה was added in the margin; וְעוֹקְ- and the final tav of מְזִיזוֹת are a second hand's writing over erasures; a vav was erased from הָפְכַתּוּ, which first read הוֹפְכַתּוּ.
sentences.say: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה אוֹמֵר אִם אֵין תּוֹרָה אֵין דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ אִם אֵין דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ אֵין תּוֹרָה אִם אֵין חָכְמָה אֵין יִרְאָה אִם אֵין יִרְאָה אֵין חָכְמָה אִם אֵין דַעַת אֵין בִּינָה אִם אֵין בִּינָה אֵין דַּעַת אִם אֵין קֶמַח אֵין תּוֹרָה אִם אֵין תּוֹרָה אֵין קֶמַח הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר כָּל שֶׁחָכְמָתוֹ מְרוּבָּה מִמַּעֲשָׂיו לְמָה הוּא דוֹמֶה לְאִילָן שֶׁנּוֹפוֹ מרובה וְשָׁרָשָׁיו מְעוּטִין וְהָרוּחַ בָּאת וְעוֹקְרַתּוּ וְהָפְכַתּוּ עַל פָּנָיו וְכָל שֶׁמַּעֲשָׂיו מְרוּבִּין מֵחָכְמָתוֹ לְמָה הוּא דוֹמֶה לְאִילָן שֶׁנּוֹפוֹ מְמוּעָט וְשָׁרָשָׁיו מְרוּבִּים אֲפִילּוּ כָל הָרוּחוֹת בָּאוֹת עָלָיו אֵין מְזִיזוֹת אוֹתוֹ מִמְּקוֹמוֹ

sentences.t: ר׳ לְעָזָר בִּן חֲסָמָה אוֹמֵ׳ קִינִּים וּפִיתְחֵי נִדָּה הֵן הֵן גּוּפֵי הֲלָכוֹת תְּקוּפוֹת וְגֵמַטַּרִיָיה פַּרְפִּרָיוֹת לַחָכְמָה:
sentences.tr: Rabi Le'azar bin Ḥasama omer: kinim u-fitḥei nida, hen hen gufei halakhot; tkufot ve-gematariya parpirayot la-ḥokhma.
sentences.l: Rabbi Leazar son of Ḥisma says: nests and openings of the menstruant, they, they are bodies of laws; seasons and geometry are side-dishes for wisdom.
sentences.i: Rabbi Leazar ben Ḥisma says: The laws of bird offerings and of the onset of menstrual impurity are the very substance of halakha. Astronomy and geometry are the side dishes of wisdom.
sentences.n: קִנִּים, 'nests', are the pairs of birds offered by a woman after childbirth and by others (Leviticus 12:8); the tractate Kinnim works out what to do when birds brought by different people get mixed up. פִּתְחֵי נִדָּה, 'openings of the menstruant', are the rules for fixing when menstrual impurity begins. Both topics demand hard reckoning, and the sage counts them the core of the law. תְּקוּפוֹת, 'cycles', is astronomy and calendar calculation; גֵּימַטְרִיָּא, from Greek geometria, here means geometry and mathematics (later the word came to mean reckoning the number-values of letters). פַּרְפְּרָאוֹת are the small dishes served around a meal. הֵן הֵן, 'they, they', is emphatic: 'these are the very'. Kaufmann spells the name לְעָזָר, Leazar, a Palestinian short form of Elazar, and points the father's name Ḥasama; the printed editions have Eliezer ben Ḥisma. Vowel points supplied by the editor where the manuscript leaves a letter bare: וּפִיתְחֵי.
sentences.say: רַבִּי לְעָזָר בִּן חֲסָמָה אוֹמֵר קִינִּים וּפִיתְחֵי נִדָּה הֵן הֵן גּוּפֵי הֲלָכוֹת תְּקוּפוֹת וְגֵמַטַּרִיָיה פַּרְפִּרָיוֹת לַחָכְמָה:
